key_insight: A reward-directed diffusion model can generate localized ship-hull refinements, but high-fidelity CFD shows that apparently improved designs may still fail at higher Froude numbers or miss physically important tradeoffs.
engineering_relevance: This work links generative design to naval architecture by showing how localized hull optimization must be validated with viscous free-surface CFD to ensure real resistance gains and physical feasibility.
method: Parametric masking limits edits to selected hull regions such as the bulbous bow and forebody while preserving global continuity.
A surrogate-assisted sequential Monte Carlo sampler searches for lower predicted calm-water resistance under displacement and stability constraints.
An automated CFD assessment compares generated hulls against an architect-refined baseline at matched KCS conditions.
evidence_signal: Validated CFD on two benchmark container ships found that the generated variant matched resistance near $F_n=0.195$ but had 45–50% higher resistance at $F_n=0.250$–$0.260$, while GenHull E was 6–8% better up to $F_n=0.240$ before reversing above $F_n=0.250$.
watch_item: The design representation could not capture a faired bulbous bow, and the reward objective omitted viscous pressure and stability terms, which may bias generated solutions.
paper_title: Localized Generative Design of Ship Hulls with Diffusion Models and High-Fidelity Assessment
